course_description:
How does literature help readers and writers imagine their place in the world, and how do the texts circulate around the globe? This course focuses on literature in English that expands the Euro-American canon and works with scales of reading and writing beyond the nation. We will read a variety of texts from different cultures and historical periods that explore how literature functions globally. You will learn about transnational, world, and planetary scales of literary analysis; think about travel and mobility; and explore the vibrant postcolonial and decolonial literary movements that challenged European imperial expansion.

ENGL2080 provides an opportunity to read writing published in English from around the world, with a particular focus on writers from outside the traditional British and American canon. We will explore the idea of world literature and how it emerged in the nineteenth century to become a major influence in twentieth- and twenty-first century writing. Students read fabulous books and learn about literary theories that analyse world writing.

Past students report: "Overall this was a really engaging and fascinating course to do, I would highly recommend it to everyone as it provides such nuanced looks into underrepresented areas of literature." In 2026, alongside past student favourites we have a refreshed middle module focused on

Employability Statement : Studying English Literature develops advanced skills in written and oral communication, critical thinking, research, and cultural knowledge and understanding. Through close reading, discussion, writing, and independent research, students learn to analyse complex ideas, construct persuasive arguments, collaborate effectively, and engage thoughtfully with diverse perspectives and literary forms.

These capabilities are highly valued across a wide range of professions, including education, government, media, publishing, law, healthcare, and the creative industries. Literary study also fosters adaptability, ethical reasoning, and the confidence to undertake long-term projects and communicate ideas clearly to different audiences.

Students are encouraged to reflect on these skills throughout their degree and to recognise how literary study prepares them for diverse career pathways, an ability to engage in lifelong learning, and to be and to be responsible citizens in pluralistic societies. ENGL2080 provides specific, research-informed training about the latter attribute in particular that will equip students to engage with rich cultural and political cultures, and will be able to demonstrate their knowledge of decolonisation and Indigenous writing.

course_aims:
To provide an informed context for reading and interpreting a selection of global literary texts published in English.

To examine world literature in relation to critical and theoretical debates.

To offer an understanding of some key historical and contemporary issues shaping contemporary world literature, the role literary texts can play in such issues, and how responses to these issuesﾠhave shifted over time.

To develop skills in locating and analysing critical materials relevant to the reception of world literature in order to produce a reasoned argument with evidence.

learning_outcomes.description: Read, interpret, and discuss world literature at university level.
Learn how literature from diverse cultures can engage productively with diverse communities and contribute to positive social change.
Present your analysis and research by demonstrating key disciplinary skills such as human-authored critical reading, textual interpretation, original analysis, and independent research.

assessment_details.task_description: Each week in tutorials we will set a 10 minute writing task, in which you write a response to a question based on that week's readings. Responses will be submitted through an online portal in Blackboard. These are marked on a pass/fail basis and can earn you 1% towards your final grade. Rationale: Consistent preparation and participation lead to better learning outcomes and more productive and enjoyable learning experiences. Through participation, humanities students gain a highly valued and distinctive skill set in human-authored critical thinking, discipline mastery, evidence-based learning, and collaboration. These skills are required by many workplaces. The ability to write on a set topic and within a short time frame is a valuable academic and vocational skill, and it helps you to track your learning and prepare for written assessment tasks. Finally, this assessment item provides basic weekly feedback throughout the semester. Read full task description Hide full task description

assessment_details.submission_guidelines:
Submit via TurnItIn.
TurnItIn Receipts:
Assignments for this course will be submitted electronically via Blackboard and using TurnItIn . Before submitting any assignments for this course you must ensure you have completed UQ's compulsory online Academic Integrity Tutorial.
When you successfully submit your assessment to TurnItIn you will see text confirming your submission is complete, before being redirected to your Assignment inbox. On this page you can:
View the name of the submitted file View date and time of the upload Resubmit your paper (if necessary) Download your submitted paper Download digital receipt.
If you cannot see your submission in your Assignment inbox you should regard your submission as unsuccessful. Students are responsible for retaining evidence of submission by the due date for all assessment items, in the required form (e.g. screenshot, email, photo, and an unaltered copy of submitted work).
If the submission was not successful:
Note the error message (preferably take a screenshot). Go to your assignment page and see if it is possible to submit again. If you cannot submit again email your course coordinator immediately with the assignment attached.
Please visit this webpage for further advice on how to submit your TurnItIn assignment .
Deferral or extension
You may be able to apply for an extension .
The maximum extension allowed is 28 days. Extensions are given in multiples of 24 hours.
Late submission
A penalty of 10% of the maximum possible mark will be deducted per 24 hours from time submission is due for up to 7 days. After 7 days, you will receive a mark of 0.

assessment_details.task_description: This assessment task will require you to prepare and deliver a (maximum) 5-minute oral presentation on Patricia Grace’s Baby No-Eyes and decolonisation. This task also gives you the opportunity to reflect critically on key issues studied in the course. Your presentation must focus on Baby No-Eyes , but you may mention in your presentation other texts and ideas that you have studied in this course that demonstrate how your disciplinary knowledge and skills have developed over the semester. Students will sign up for an allocated time during the examination period to meet with course staff and deliver a 4-5 minute presentation based on an oral assessment guide that will be available in Blackboard. Following your presentation, up to two additional questions will be asked to enable the student to amplify or clarify their presentation. We will build oral skills and confidence throughout the tutorials. Note: presentations will be recorded (audio only). Read full task description Hide full task description

policies_and_procedures: University policies and procedures apply to all aspects of student life. As a UQ student, you must comply with University-wide and program-specific requirements, including the: Student Code of Conduct Policy Student Integrity and Misconduct Policy and Procedure Assessment Procedure Examinations Procedure Reasonable Adjustments for Students Policy and Procedure AI for Assessment Guide Recording of Teaching Policy and Procedure Learn more about UQ policies on my.UQ and the Policy and Procedure Library . Course guidelines Communication Expectations While you are a student at UQ, all communication must be conducted according to the UQ Student Code of Conduct . The UQ Library has a helpful Communicate and collaborate online module . Email is the primary way for you to send messages to, and receive information from, the School and our staff. You must use your UQ email address (not a private address) to communicate with staff. You should add a clear subject line, including course code, and a 2-3 word statement. You can send email at any time, however, please do not expect responses outside normal working hours (Monday to Friday from ~8am to ~5pm). Emails that constitute bullying, harassment or discrimination against staff contravene the Student Code of Conduct. Emails like this will be reported to the University, and the matter will be pursued as misconduct. Learning activities
